ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In the device shown in the figure, regions I and III have uniform electric fields directed vertically upward and horizontally to the right, respectively, with electric field strengths of $E$ and $\frac{E}{2}$. Region II has a uniform horizontal magnetic field directed outward, with a magnetic induction strength of $B$. A negatively charged particle with mass $m$ and charge $q$ (neglecting gravity) is horizontally injected into the electric field from point $M$ directly above the left boundary point $O$ with an initial velocity $v_{0}$. It enters the magnetic field in region II at point $A$ on the horizontal boundary line $OP$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to $OP$, and then enters the uniform electric field in region III perpendicular to the vertical boundary $CD$.

1. The radius of the particle's trajectory in the uniform magnetic field in region II.
2. (2) The width of the uniform magnetic field region $O P$.
3. (3) The time it takes for the particle to travel from point $M$ until its velocity first becomes zero.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, above the dashed boundary on the left side there is point M, and M is directly above point O; region I is located above OP, with vertically upward electric-field arrows drawn and labeled E, and the particle enters from M with a horizontally rightward initial velocity v0. Point A is located on the horizontal boundary OP; in the figure, the velocity direction entering the lower dotted region II from A is toward the lower right, and makes an angle of 60° with OP; region II uses black dots to indicate that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface outward, and is labeled B. The dashed boundary on the right side is CD, and P is near the intersection point of OP and CD; region III is on the right side of CD, with horizontally rightward electric-field arrows drawn and labeled E/2. The problem statement also explains that when the particle enters region III it is perpendicular to the vertical boundary CD, therefore the velocity entering region III is horizontally rightward. Then reason: let q denote the magnitude of the negative charge. In region I, the electric field is upward, the negative particle is acted on by the electric-field force downward, and the magnitude of the acceleration is a1=qE/m. The velocity in the horizontal direction remains vx=v0, and the vertically downward velocity increases from 0. At A, the velocity makes an angle of 60° with OP, so tan60°=vy/v0, giving vy=√3 v0. Therefore the speed at A is vA=sqrt(v0^2+3v0^2)=2v0, the time is t1=vy/a1=√3 m v0/(qE), and the horizontal distance OA=v0 t1=√3 m v0^2/(qE). In region II, the magnetic field only changes the direction of velocity and does not change the speed, so the speed is still 2v0, and the radius of circular motion is R=m(2v0)/(qB)=2mv0/(qB). From the velocity direction being toward the lower right and making 60° with the horizontal when entering the magnetic field, to the velocity being horizontally rightward when entering region III, the velocity direction changes by 60°, corresponding to a central angle π/3. The time of motion in the magnetic field is t2=(π/3)/(qB/m)=πm/(3qB). According to circular-arc geometry, the horizontal projection from A to the right boundary is R sin60°=(2mv0/(qB))(√3/2)=√3 m v0/(qB). Therefore the width of the magnetic-field region is OP=OA+R sin60°=√3 m v0^2/(qE)+√3 m v0/(qB)=√3 m v0/q · (v0/E+1/B). In region III, the particle enters horizontally rightward with 2v0, the electric field is rightward while the negative particle is acted on by a force to the left, and the magnitude of the acceleration is a3=q(E/2)/m=qE/(2m); the time required for the velocity to be zero for the first time is t3=2v0/a3=4mv0/(qE). The total time is t=t1+t2+t3=(√3+4)mv0/(qE)+πm/(3qB).
